title: Are the Benefits of Organic Food Underrated or Overrated?
summary: NutritionFacts weighs organic benefits: fewer residues and less cadmium, but organic junk food is still junk and produce intake matters most.

assertions.quote: Organic fruits and vegetables have fewer pesticides
even the levels on conventional produce are generally well below accepted limits

verdicts.note: Regulators deem sub-MRL residues safe, but some samples exceed MRLs (up to 6% of spinach), safety of some pesticides and mixtures below MRL is disputed, and authors say the health benefit of lower exposure is impossible to estimate.

About 1.5% of EU samples exceeded the acute reference dose, and recent reviews conclude prenatal organophosphate exposure at levels common in the general population likely harms children's neurodevelopment.

Of 9,872 nationally representative 2024 samples, over 99% were below EPA tolerances and 42.3% had no detectable residue; this shows tolerance compliance (set at 'reasonable certainty of no harm') rather than measuring health outcomes, and samples were not split by organic label.

For the ten most detected pesticides on each 2010 Dirty Dozen crop, RfDs exceeded mean exposure in every case and by over 1000-fold in more than 90% of comparisons; limited to 2004-2008 data, top-ten pesticides and mean (not high-end) exposure.

In three US cohorts of health professionals (180,316 people, 23,678 cancers over up to 18 years), intake of high-pesticide-residue fruit and vegetables, ranked from USDA PDP data, was not associated with total or site-specific cancer (HR 0.99 per daily serving); exposure was estimated, not measured, and specific chemicals are not ruled out.

In the same three US cohorts (160,880 people, 27,026 deaths), at least 4 daily servings of low-residue fruit and vegetables went with 36% lower mortality while high-residue intake showed no benefit (HR 0.93, 0.81-1.07), which the authors read as residues offsetting the benefit; observational, exposure estimated from PDP data, residual confounding possible.

Among 325 women in IVF treatment, the top quartile of high-residue fruit and vegetable intake had 26% lower probability of live birth than the bottom quartile, suggesting harm within typical dietary exposure; a small fertility-clinic cohort, exposure estimated, and the authors call it a first report needing confirmation.

EFSA's cumulative assessment of 2014-2016 EU monitoring data for 10 populations concluded that combined exposure to pesticides with acute nervous-system effects stays below the regulatory threshold at the 99.9th percentile, with over 99% certainty for adults but only 80-95% for some toddler and child groups; it covers two nervous-system effects only.

assertions.quote: something that isn't necessarily taken into account in the pesticide approval process

verdicts.note: Review states additive/synergistic effects of pesticide mixtures have been documented and safety testing of mixtures is not required in regulatory pesticide approval.
Regulators judge residues by individual-pesticide MRLs, about 30% of samples carry multiple residues, and a main criticism is that approval does not require testing of mixtures.

About 25% of EU samples carry residues of more than one pesticide but EFSA reports include no cumulative risk calculation, and the review notes concern that risk assessment is inadequate for mixed exposures.

PDP multi-residue data are supplied to EPA for cumulative assessments of pesticides with a common mechanism of toxicity (39.8% of samples held more than one pesticide), so combined effects are assessed within mechanism groups, though not for arbitrary mixtures.

EFSA ran a cumulative risk assessment of dietary residues, adding doses across pesticides with a common effect and computing a combined margin of exposure at each percentile, so EU regulators do assess combined effects within effect groups.

assertions.quote: organic foods have more antioxidant, phytonutrients
organic crops only have about half the cadmium

verdicts.note: Weighted and unweighted meta-analyses both found significantly lower Cd in organic crops (mean difference -48%, wide CI), significant for cereals but not fruit or vegetables separately; GRADE reliability moderate.

Meta-analyses conflict (Smith-Spangler no difference; corrected Baranski 30% higher in conventional), the difference holds only in cereals, and long-term paired studies are lacking; plausible because mineral phosphate fertiliser carries cadmium.

assertions.quote: people, for example, falsely judge organic Oreo cookies to have fewer calories than conventional Oreos

verdicts.note: Experiments on the organic halo show people rate organic-labelled snacks as lower in calories.

assertions.quote: we should never let concern about pesticides stop us from stuffing our face with as many fruits and vegetables as possible
